title: From Church to Nature: the Prussian Officer Who Became the Nature-Preacher
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Officer's Son: Königsberg to Stolp

stops.name: Königsberg, birth in the garrison city
stops.date_confidence: attested; the German national authority file (GND 116936053) gives the day exactly. The coordinate is the city centre, no birth address having been located.
stops.campa: On the sixth of August a son is born in Königsberg to an officer of the Prussian army who will end his working life in the postal administration. They enter him as Johannes Friedrich Guttzeit. The city is Kant's city and the easternmost of the kingdom's great towns, a harbour and a garrison at once, and the family belongs to the class that moves when the service says move. The national authority file fixes this date to the day. Eighty-two years later the same file will fail to fix the date of his death at all.
suggested_refs: The Guttzeit authority record, GND 116936053, Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek
sources: Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek, authority record gnd/116936053

stops.name: Breslau, the first of the postings
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The sources name the childhood towns without years; the date is a placeholder chosen only to order the childhood, and the sequence of the moves is not established.
stops.campa: The father's postings carry the household south to Breslau, capital of Silesia. The boy is six, or he is nine; the biographical notes give the towns and withhold the years, and the order they are printed in, Breslau, Neuruppin, Höxter, Königsberg again, is the compilers' order rather than a documented sequence. The quarters belong to the service and not to the family. Somebody in an office decides when they are vacated, and the household is told. He will spend the middle of his life walking from one German town to the next with what he owns on his back.
suggested_refs: The Prussian postal service registers of officer-officials, Silesian district

stops.name: Neuruppin, another garrison, another unpacking
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; undated placeholder. No source gives the year of this leg or its position among the childhood moves.
stops.campa: Another transfer, another garrison town: Neuruppin in the Mark Brandenburg, a place of barracks and of the cheap coloured broadsheets that carried Prussian battle scenes into kitchens across the kingdom. The Guttzeit household unpacks and will pack again. Nothing of the boy himself survives from these years, no schoolbook, no letter, no anecdote told back by a classmate. He is somewhere between seven and twelve, and the record holds only the name of the town.
suggested_refs: The Neuruppin Bilderbogen presses, chief supplier of popular military imagery in Prussia

stops.name: Höxter, the last station before the cadet house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; undated placeholder. The childhood itinerary is reconstructed in outline only, and the order of Breslau, Neuruppin and Höxter is not fixed by any source.
stops.campa: Höxter on the Weser, a Westphalian town of half-timbered fronts under the shadow of an abbey older than Prussia, is the last of the childhood stations the record preserves. Then the moving stops, because the boy is handed to an institution that will do his moving for him. Four German towns before the age of thirteen is what the list establishes; how long each of them lasted, and in what order, it does not. The abbey is Corvey, on the Weser at the edge of the town. No source says whether the boy was ever taken inside it.
suggested_refs: The abbey of Corvey at Höxter, on the Weser

stops.name: The Prussian cadet corps, a boy handed to the army
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact and the approximate age (de.wikipedia). No source names the cadet house or its city; the coordinate is Berlin, administrative centre of the Prussian cadet system, and is a placeholder rather than an attested site.
stops.campa: At about thirteen he enters a Prussian Kadettenanstalt, the machinery by which officers' sons are turned into officers. The regime is drill and mathematics, French and religion, and above all the graded obedience of a boy army, in which every man above you is addressed as Herr. He will spend his forties refusing to speak that word, on the grounds that it carries domination inside it and cannot be cleaned. He is thirteen. He learns it the way the rest of the room learns it, and nobody in the building is offering a second grammar.
suggested_refs: Records of the Prussian cadet institutions, 1866 intake

stops.name: Stolp in Pomerania, the officer's years
stops.date_confidence: the commission of 1871 is attested (de.wikipedia); the Stolp posting as Bezirksadjutant and the claim of Franco-Prussian War service are tradition, repeated in later Lebensreform and Hauptmann-adjacent sketches and not verified against Prussian military rolls. Some of that literature makes him a Bavarian officer, which the Prussian record contradicts.
stops.campa: He is commissioned in 1871, the year the war with France ends and the Empire is proclaimed. Tradition puts him through that war and then into a long stint as Bezirksadjutant at Stolp in Pomerania, an administrative posting, muster rolls and district paperwork rather than the field. A commission dated 1871 leaves little room for service in a war that ends the same year, and a strand of the later literature makes him a Bavarian officer, which the Prussian record contradicts. The Stolp district rolls for 1871 to 1879 would settle all of it. They have not been consulted.
suggested_refs: Prussian military rolls for the Stolp district, 1871-1879, not yet consulted
sources: later Lebensreform and Hauptmann-adjacent biographical sketches (unverified, contradictory)

stops.name: Stolp, the commission resigned
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and cause: de.wikipedia gives one cause only, 'Nach dem Tod seiner Eltern quittierte er 1879 den Militärdienst.' A tradition adding personal illness circulates in the secondary literature but no source for it has been located, and it is recorded here as unsourced rather than as a competing account. The place of the resignation is not documented; the pin is his last attested posting.
stops.campa: His parents die and he leaves the army. That is the whole of the attested cause: after the death of his parents he quit military service in 1879. He is twenty-six, trained for one profession and released from it, with no property, no town, and no household left to return to. A tradition in the secondary literature adds an illness to the cause; no source for it has been found, and it is recorded here as unsourced rather than as a rival account. Two years later he is in Italy.
suggested_refs: Prussian officer discharge records, 1879

segments.name: Italy, and the Turn from Church to Nature

stops.name: Italy, two years and a change of diet
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the journey and its approximate length (de.wikipedia, roughly two years, 1881 to 1883). No Italian city is documented; the coordinate is a national placeholder, not an attested landmark.
stops.campa: For roughly two years he is in Italy. No city is recorded, no address, no companion, no route. The result is recorded: he comes back a vegetarian and a believer in natural living, and the biographers who cannot say where he was in Italy are unanimous that Italy is where the turn happened. Educated Germans of his generation went south by the hundred and came back with a taste in architecture. This one came back having changed what he ate. What he ate it with, and in whose company, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: German vegetarian society correspondence of the early 1880s

stops.name: Berlin, Von der Kirche zur Natur
stops.date_confidence: the work is attested; the year is not. Literaturport dates it 1882, other catalogues 1881, and the contradiction is left open here rather than resolved. Place of publication pinned to Berlin, where his subsequent activity is documented.
stops.campa: His first substantial book carries the whole programme in its title: From the Church to Nature, expression of the chief spiritual current of our age. The argument is not that the sacred is a fraud but that it has been kept in the wrong building. It is to be moved out of the church and into the woods, the diet, the body, the daylight. Ten years after taking a commission from the King of Prussia, he has published a book against the established church. The catalogues cannot agree on the year: Literaturport says 1882, others say 1881, and no reachable source resolves them.
suggested_refs: Von der Kirche zur Natur. Ausdruck der Hauptgeistesströmung unseres Zeitalters, first edition

stops.name: Berlin, Unsinn und Unmoral im Alten Testament
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. de.wikipedia gives the title as 'Unsinn und Unmoral im Alten Testament'; the 1882 date, the confiscation of early editions and the resulting imprisonment come from Guttzeit's own later retrospective account and have not been verified against any catalogue or court record.
stops.campa: The companion volume goes straight at scripture: Nonsense and Immorality in the Old Testament. By his own later account the early editions were seized and his religious writings brought him prison, and no catalogue entry or court file has been found to confirm either half of that. He will rework the same material for thirty years and publish the last version, gentler and more mystical, in 1914. His quarrel with the Bible is already three years old when he first hears of the painter Karl Wilhelm Diefenbach.
suggested_refs: Prussian confiscation and blasphemy prosecution records of the 1880s, not located
sources: Guttzeit's own later retrospective account (self-report, unverified)

stops.name: Berlin, the Bund der Pythagoräer founded
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year, founders and city; no day or month is given in any source, and the January date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: In Berlin he joins Robert Springer, Otto Rabe and Karl Max Engelmann to found the Bund der Pythagoräer. The name is a claim about ancestry: meat-abstention is not a fad of the 1880s but the discipline of a school two and a half thousand years old. Springer's Enkarpa, out the same year, ties abstention to Pythagorean purification and to compassion for animals. The reform does not stop at the plate: it legislates dwelling, clothing and the ordinary conduct of a day. They print their motto in a spelling reformed to their own taste, Grundsaz for Grundsatz, Zil for Ziel, one more inherited convention taken apart on the way to the table.
stops.quote: Unser Grundsaz: Ni Fleisch, ni Fisch! (Pythagoras). Unser Zil: Mässigkeit und Stärke, Weisheit und Libe! (Plato)
stops.quote_source: Motto of the Bund der Pythagoräer, 1884, in the group's own reform orthography, quoted at gusto-graeser.de (Hermann Müller's archive).
suggested_refs: Otto Rabe, Di hohe Kulturbedeutung der fleisch- und blutlosen Ernärung des Menschen (Berlin, 1885), first pamphlet of the Bund der Pythagoräer
sources: Hermann Müller, 'Bruder-Bund und Pythagoraeer-Bund', gusto-graeser.de PDF

stops.name: Berlin, the Internationaler Bund für konsequente Humanität
stops.date_confidence: attested that the same four men are recorded founding a body of this name in the same year (de.wikipedia, 'Robert Springer (Schriftsteller)'). No source resolves whether it duplicates, subsumes or stands apart from the Pythagoräer-Bund. The June date is an unattested placeholder chosen only to separate this stop from the January founding.
stops.campa: The same four names appear again in the same year under a different letterhead: the International League for Consistent Humanity. Consistent is the operative word, and the consistency is the whole demand, one rule carried without exception to the table, the household, the wardrobe and the way one man addresses another. Whether this body is the Pythagoreans renamed, the Pythagoreans plus a wider circle, or a second society running alongside the first, no source says.
suggested_refs: Founding papers of the Internationaler Bund für konsequente Humanität, Berlin 1884, not located

stops.name: Berlin, the death of Robert Springer
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Robert Springer, born Berlin 23 November 1816, died Berlin 21 October 1885.
stops.campa: Robert Springer dies in Berlin, thirteen months after the founding, at sixty-eight, in the city he was born in. He was the eldest of the four and the author of the book that gave the brotherhood its argument, and with him gone the society loses the man who held it to Pythagoras. Guttzeit is thirty-two and takes what is left of it. Rabe and Engelmann have occupations. He has a book against the Old Testament, no income anyone has recorded, and the whole of his day.
suggested_refs: Robert Springer, Enkarpa (1884)

stops.name: Berlin, the Bruder-Bund and the journal Der Bruder
stops.date_confidence: the renaming and the journal are attested; the year is contested. de.wikipedia and the gusto-graeser.de PDF put it in 1885, immediately after Springer's death; Engelmann's own file in this corpus dates the renaming and the launch of Der Bruder to 1886. A further strain: Diefenbach's letter of June 1885 already speaks of reading the Bruder-Bund's journal, four months before Springer died. The contradiction is flagged, not resolved. The November date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Pythagoras comes off the letterhead. Guttzeit gives the society a new name and a new direction, Bund für volle Menschlichkeit, League for Full Humanity, with two words under it: Verbrüderung and Vernatürlichung, brotherhood and naturalisation. The journal is called Der Bruder, and the members address each other as du. Guttzeit will not say Herr at all. Every use of it, he holds, rehearses a relation of master to servant. He spent thirteen years in barracks where the word was compulsory in every sentence spoken upward.
stops.quote: Bund für volle Menschlichkeit. Verbrüderung, Vernatürlichung
stops.quote_source: The name and motto Guttzeit gave the reorganised society after Springer's death, quoted in the gusto-graeser.de PDF on the 1885 Bruder-Bund. The journal's own full title is 'Der Bruder. Zeitschrift des Bundes für volle Menschlichkeit'.
suggested_refs: Der Bruder. Zeitschrift des Bundes für volle Menschlichkeit, surviving issues
sources: Hermann Müller, gusto-graeser.de PDF on the 1885 Bruder-Bund

segments.name: Höllriegelskreuth: the Sister, the Painter, and Christmas Eve

stops.name: Berlin, the painter's letter
stops.date_confidence: attested that Diefenbach opened contact with the Bruder-Bund, read its journal, wanted to be written about in it, and asked Guttzeit to visit him. The 22 June 1885 date belongs to Diefenbach's letter to Max Engelmann of the same milieu; the letter to Guttzeit is undated in the reachable source and is placed here alongside it. The pin is Berlin, where Guttzeit receives it, not Munich-Thalkirchen, where Diefenbach writes.
stops.campa: A letter arrives from a painter outside Munich. Karl Wilhelm Diefenbach has been reading Der Bruder, wants the journal to write about him, and asks Guttzeit to come and see him. His complaint is that the reform movements of the age have no centre and spend their strength fighting each other, and that he can supply one. It is an invitation to stop editing a journal in Berlin and come and live inside somebody else's picture of a redeemed world. Guttzeit's sister goes first.
stops.quote: Es hat allen Reformbestrebungen unserer Zeit der zu ihrem Gedeihen absolut nötige innere Zusammenhang, ein fester mächtiger Zentralpunkt ausserhalb der "Gesellschaft" (intra ecclesia nulla salus!) gefehlt, alle Reform-"Parteien" bekämpfen sich gegenseitig.
stops.quote_source: Karl Wilhelm Diefenbach, letter inviting Guttzeit to visit him, 1885, quoted in the gusto-graeser.de PDF on the 1885 Bruder-Bund.
suggested_refs: Diefenbach's letter to Max Engelmann, Munich-Thalkirchen, 22 June 1885, of the same correspondence
sources: Hermann Müller, gusto-graeser.de PDF on the 1885 Bruder-Bund

stops.name: Höllriegelskreuth, the sister arrives and is renamed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: gusto-graeser.info records Elisabeth Guttzeit's arrival at Höllriegelskreuth on 10 July 1885 and Diefenbach's renaming of her as Fidelis. The coordinate is corrected here to 48.0431 / 11.5094, Höllriegelskreuth being a locality of Pullach im Isartal; three earlier working values in the research pool were all wrong by two to three kilometres.
stops.campa: Elisabeth Guttzeit arrives at the painter's community above the Isar, south of Munich, on the tenth of July. Diefenbach takes her name away and gives her another: Fidelis, the faithful one. That is how the household works. The master assigns the names, the diet, the hours, the clothes, and the members receive them. She stays. Her brother, who has spent the year telling a readership that no man should be called Herr by another, comes down from Berlin two months later and joins the household on those terms.
suggested_refs: Schirn Kunsthalle, 'Artists and Prophets' wall panels on the Diefenbach circle
sources: Schirn museum press panels PDF on the Diefenbach circle

stops.name: Höllriegelskreuth, secretary to Diefenbach
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the arrival (museum research on the Diefenbach circle; de.wikipedia). The length of the secretaryship and the course of the falling-out are not documented in detail.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of September Guttzeit follows his sister and takes up work as Diefenbach's secretary and keeper of the household record. The exchange runs both ways. He adopts elements of the painter's apostolic dress, the coarse robe and the bare head, and carries them out of Bavaria for the next twenty years; his own vocabulary of brotherhood runs into Diefenbach's developing Humanitas. He has been a Bezirksadjutant. He knows how to keep another man's papers in order. He does not last four months.
suggested_refs: Diefenbach's household books from Höllriegelskreuth, 1885
sources: Schirn museum press panels PDF on the Diefenbach circle

stops.name: Höllriegelskreuth, gone by Christmas Eve
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That Diefenbach found fault with him and that he was gone by the end of 1885 is well supported; the specific Christmas Eve date comes only from the sympathetic Graeser-circle literature and should be read as probable rather than independently established.
stops.campa: Diefenbach finds fault with him, and on Christmas Eve he walks out of the community and back into the winter. He is thirty-two. Inside twelve months he has lost a brotherhood's founder, a journal's subscribers and a patron, and he leaves with a robe, a pair of sandals and the arguments he brought in with him. After this he stops trying to run an organisation and starts walking. The date comes from the sympathetic literature and only from there. Nobody at all records the quarrel.
suggested_refs: gusto-graeser.info, 'Guttzeit', the Diefenbach episode
sources: gusto-graeser.info / gusto-graeser.de (Graeser-circle sourcing, flagged as sympathetic)

stops.name: Zurich, Gerhart Hauptmann sees an apostle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and city: '1888 lernte er in Zürich Gerhart Hauptmann kennen.' An earlier working date of 20 May 1888 was back-derived from Hauptmann's epithet Pfingstapostel and is dropped here; the word characterises the man, not the calendar, and no source places the meeting at Pentecost.
stops.campa: For two years he has been on the road as a Naturprediger, lecturing to vegetarian and natural-healing societies and, by some accounts, comparing his own wandering to that of Ahasuerus. In Zurich a young dramatist called Gerhart Hauptmann meets him and never forgets it: coarse haircloth, sandals, reddish hair to the shoulders, a cord about a bare head. Hauptmann's word for him is Pfingstapostel, a Pentecost apostle. Two years later he will put him in a book, and Guttzeit will object.
stops.quote: Niemals habe ich eine so augenfällige, gegenwartsstarke Illustration evangelischer Vorgaenge vorher und nachher erlebt. Es war eine wahrhaft heilige Szene, die durch kein Oberammergau zu erreichen ist.
stops.quote_source: Gerhart Hauptmann on the Zurich meeting, quoted in de.wikipedia.org, 'Johannes Friedrich Guttzeit'; the description of the dress and hair is from Hauptmann's Das Abenteuer meiner Jugend. Secondhand quotation of Hauptmann, the primary notebook text not consulted.
suggested_refs: Gerhart Hauptmann, Der Apostel (1890), whose protagonist combines characteristics of Guttzeit and Diefenbach
Barbara Neymeyr, 'Imitatio Christi als fixe Idee. Pathographie und Intertextualität in Gerhart Hauptmanns novellistischer Studie Der Apostel', Weimarer Beiträge 68 (2022) 3, pp.390-415
Gerhart Hauptmann, Notiz-Kalender 1889 bis 1891, ed. Machatzke, pp.278f., recording Guttzeit's protest against the portrait
sources: Gerhart Hauptmann, Das Abenteuer meiner Jugend

stops.name: Berlin, prosecuted for grober Unfug
stops.date_confidence: the prosecution is attested for 1890; the city is not documented anywhere reachable and the Berlin pin is a placeholder. The acquittal reported by later accounts is unsourced: the word freigesprochen appears nowhere in the cited de.wikipedia article, and this element is downgraded to reconstruction.
stops.campa: The state prosecutes him for grober Unfug, gross public nuisance, on account of how he is dressed. Not for what the pamphlets say, not for the attacks on scripture, but for the robe, the sandals and the hair, worn in a German street in 1890. The body is the argument, and it is answered in a courtroom. Two books come out of the charge, one in 1893 and one in 1914, and both are about clothes. Later accounts say he was acquitted, though none of them names a court or a date, and the word does not appear in the record consulted here.
suggested_refs: Guttzeit, Auch ein heiliger Rock (1893), and Die Tyrannei der Mode (1914), both arising from this prosecution

stops.name: Stuttgart, Der volle Mensch
stops.date_confidence: the Stuttgart residence is reconstruction: the sources name it among his 1890s addresses without dates, and the residence sequence for the decade is imperfectly reconstructed. The publication of Der volle Mensch is dated 1891 in the working bibliography.
stops.campa: Somewhere in the wandering years he lives at Stuttgart, one of a string of addresses no source puts in order. Out of it comes the phrase that will carry everything else: Der volle Mensch oder Freier Fortschritt zum Ideale, the full human being. The claim is that the human being available in 1891 is a partial one, cut down by church, barracks, school, tailor and marriage law, and that the missing portion can be recovered inside a single lifetime by a man who sets about it. Whether he thought he had recovered his own, the book does not say.
suggested_refs: Der volle Mensch oder Freier Fortschritt zum Ideale (1891)
sources: working bibliography reconstructed from library catalogues

stops.name: Söflingen near Ulm, the pamphlets against the rod
stops.date_confidence: the Söflingen residence is reconstruction, part of the same undated 1890s sequence. Both 1892 titles come from the working bibliography reconstructed from library catalogues and have not been checked against a copy.
stops.campa: From Söflingen, outside Ulm, two pamphlets go out in the same year. One is Das Prügeln in der Schule, beating in school as a danger to education and morality. The other is Über Soldatenmisshandlungen und Beschwerderecht, on the mistreatment of soldiers and the right of complaint. He was in the second institution from thirteen, and both pamphlets put the same question: what an adult with authority may do to a body in his charge. Neither title has been checked against a surviving copy. Both come from catalogue reconstruction.
suggested_refs: Das Prügeln in der Schule (1892)
Über Soldatenmisshandlungen und Beschwerderecht (1892)
sources: working bibliography reconstructed from library catalogues

stops.name: Dresden-Loschwitz, the vineyard slope above the Elbe
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the date; the residence at Dresden-Loschwitz is attested by local research, and de.wikipedia additionally names a Viktoriastrasse address in Dresden around this period. The coordinate is corrected here to the de.wikipedia value for Loschwitz, 51.0539 / 13.8150; three different working values circulated in the research pool.
stops.campa: He settles on the Elbe slope at Loschwitz, a vineyard suburb of Dresden full of artists and cheap rooms, and the publishing begins in earnest. Corporal punishment, the mistreatment of soldiers, fashion, spiritualism, love, immortality, the raising of children, marriage, free love, love between people of the same sex: over the next decade there is almost no domain of German respectability he leaves alone. On the covers is his own emblem, an apple breaking a sword, and his word for the order he is attacking, Schlachthaus-Zivilisation.
suggested_refs: Uwe Wolfram, 'Johannes Guttzeit, Naturprediger am Elbhang', Elbhang-Kurier 3/2014, pp.12-13

stops.name: Loschwitz, Naturrecht oder Verbrechen?
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the date of first circulation. Standard bibliographies, Robert Beachy among them, date the work to 1899 or 1900; a booksellers' trade advertisement proves circulation by 1897, and an 1899 bibliography of homosexual literature already lists it, which makes the later dates too late. 1895 is the working reconstruction, not an attested imprint.
stops.campa: Naturrecht oder Verbrechen? Über Liebe zum gleichen Geschlecht. Natural right or crime? On love for the same sex. He answers his own title in the first direction, years before the standard histories of the German homosexual emancipation movement place him in it. The dating matters because the histories are wrong about it: a trade advertisement has the book circulating by 1897 and a bibliography lists it in 1899. Nothing in any source establishes Guttzeit's own orientation, and the Graeser-circle claim that he was homosexual rests on nothing reachable.
suggested_refs: Bibliographie der homosexuellen Literatur (1899), listing the work
Robert Beachy, 'The German Invention of Homosexuality', Journal of Modern History 82 (2010), which dates it 1900
sources: regis-schlagdenhauffen.eu, 1899 bibliography of homosexual literature PDF
Robert Beachy, Journal of Modern History 82 (2010)

stops.name: Loschwitz, Meine Ehe
stops.date_confidence: the work and its 1896 date come from the working bibliography reconstructed from library catalogues. No civil marriage certificate has been located for either of Guttzeit's marriages, so the autobiographical warrant of the title cannot be checked against a register.
stops.campa: Meine Ehe. Aufhebung des Gegensatzes zwischen Ehe und freier Liebe. My marriage: the abolition of the opposition between marriage and free love. He takes the two positions that the 1890s treat as enemies and argues that a man may hold both, and he does it in the first person, using his own household as the demonstration. Which household this is, and married to whom, the record does not say anywhere. No certificate of marriage has been found for any of it, in this decade or in the next.
suggested_refs: Meine Ehe. Aufhebung des Gegensatzes zwischen Ehe und freier Liebe (1896)
sources: working bibliography reconstructed from library catalogues

stops.name: Loschwitz, the forty theses
stops.date_confidence: usually dated 1898, though some material suggests an earlier version circulated; the title and content are summarised in de.wikipedia and in secondary Lebensreform scholarship rather than checked against a copy.
stops.campa: Was will der Naturprediger? Forty theses of pure humanity, and the clearest thing he ever wrote. A natural culture. Humanity as one family. Neither servants nor masters, weder Knechte noch Herren. Women out of the old slavery. Children spared useless schooling. Animals recognised as beings that feel. Natural rights to life, health, love and joy. Thirty-nine absolute demands, and then a fortieth that undercuts the form of the list: let nobody condemn anybody, because nobody is infallible.
stops.quote: Keiner den Andern verdamme, weil Keiner unfehlbar ist
stops.quote_source: Johannes Guttzeit, Was will der Naturprediger? 40 Lehrsätze des reinen Menschentums, closing thesis, quoted at gusto-graeser.info, 'Guttzeit'
suggested_refs: Was will der Naturprediger? 40 Lehrsätze des reinen Menschentums (c.1898)

stops.name: Loschwitz, the doctrine carried to the Himmelhof
stops.date_confidence: attested that Anton Losert and two other Guttzeit followers entered Diefenbach's Himmelhof community near Vienna in 1898, preached a radical primitive-Christian ethic including the rejection of money, won the young Gusto Graeser to it and took part in a rebellion against Diefenbach. Guttzeit himself is not recorded at the Himmelhof, so this stop sits at his own residence rather than in Vienna. The June date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Three of his followers, Anton Losert among them, walk into Diefenbach's second community at the Himmelhof outside Vienna, carrying the Loschwitz doctrine in its hardest form: primitive Christianity, no property, no money at all. They convert a young Bohemian named Gusto Graeser and then help lead a revolt against the painter. Thirteen years after his own quarrel with Diefenbach, his argument arrives at Diefenbach's door in other men's mouths. Guttzeit is at Loschwitz. He is not recorded at the Himmelhof at any point, and Losert, who did the travelling, has no file of his own.
suggested_refs: Ulrich Linse, Barfüßige Propheten (1983), on the Himmelhof rebellion

stops.name: Dresden, Alma Guttzeit in the exhibition catalogue
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. An Alma Guttzeit is independently documented in Dresden publishing on children in the Dresden art exhibition; her association with Johannes as his wife rests on family and Graeser-circle tradition, and no civil marriage certificate has been located. The specialist tradition placing the two of them running an alternative book trade near Trieste after 1900 is recorded here as tradition only.
stops.campa: In the Dresden art world of 1899 an Alma Guttzeit publishes on the children in the city's exhibition. The tradition makes her his wife, and puts the two of them after 1900 running an alternative book trade down near Trieste. What exists in the record is a woman with his surname writing about art in the city where he was living, and no certificate of marriage anywhere. The standard biography separately has him marrying for a second time in 1905, which leaves the first marriage undated and unnamed.
suggested_refs: The 1899 Dresden art exhibition catalogue and its notices
sources: Dresden art-exhibition publication record (yumpu.com Käthe Kollwitz document)

stops.name: Hoyerswerda, ordered to report to prison
stops.date_confidence: attested by Guttzeit's own autobiographical notice in his journal, summer 1900, which gives the date and place of the order and the three-month term.
stops.campa: He is to present himself at Hoyerswerda on the sixth of April to begin three months' imprisonment for Beschimpfung der jüdischen Religion, insulting the Jewish religion, incurred by his attacks on the Old Testament and what he called its Blut- und Eisenreligion, its religion of blood and iron. He does not present himself. He lectures, publishes, arranges his move south. His own defence is that no Jew had felt insulted. That is the defendant speaking, and it settles nothing: whether his attacks on the Old Testament ran with the antisemitism of 1900 or across it is a question nobody has yet worked through his texts to answer.
suggested_refs: The Prussian court file for the Beschimpfung prosecution, not located
sources: Guttzeit's autobiographical notice in Der Neue Mensch, summer 1900

stops.name: Loschwitz, Der Neue Mensch begins
stops.date_confidence: attested by Guttzeit's own surviving notice, which marks volume 1 as May to June 1900. This corrects the standard biographies, which place the journal's start in 1901. A photograph on gusto-graeser.info captioned to Der Neue Mensch and dated 1900 supports the earlier date independently.
stops.campa: With a prison term outstanding he starts a journal. Der Neue Mensch, the new human being, volume one dated May to June 1900, fifteen years after Der Bruder and with nobody left of the Berlin four to help him run it. The standard biographies put its beginning in 1901; his own notice, which survives, says otherwise, and a photograph captioned to the journal is dated 1900 as well. In the first volume he sets out in verse where his commission comes from, and from where it does not.
stops.quote: Von keiner Sekte komm' ich ausgesandt, / Und keine Macht hat mich in ihrem Solde; / Mir schrieb kein Kirchenrat auf meine Kanzel, / Was ich zu lehren, zu verschweigen habe. / Allein der Gott in meiner eig'nen Brust / Hat mich berufen, vor euch hinzutreten,
stops.quote_source: Johannes Guttzeit, verse in Der Neue Mensch, 1. Jg. (1900), quoted at gusto-graeser.info, 'Guttzeit'. The source prints a typographic apostrophe in eig'nen and spaces the word Allein letter by letter for emphasis.
suggested_refs: Der Neue Mensch, volume 1, May-June 1900

stops.name: Breslau, arrested within the hour
stops.date_confidence: attested by Guttzeit's own contemporary account in Der Neue Mensch, summer 1900, a firmer evidentiary basis than the short biographies provide.
stops.campa: Three months after the day he was told to report, the Breslau prosecutor catches up with him. He is arrested within an hour of the instruction being issued and put on the road south to Ratibor. He is forty-six years old. Breslau is one of the towns his father was posted to when he was a boy, one of the four he lived in before the cadet house took him, and he passes through it now under escort, on his way to serve three months for what he wrote about a book. He records the whole of it himself, in his own journal, that summer.
suggested_refs: Guttzeit's autobiographical notice in Der Neue Mensch, summer 1900
sources: Guttzeit's autobiographical notice in Der Neue Mensch, summer 1900

stops.name: Ratibor, the three months served
stops.date_confidence: attested by Guttzeit's own journal notice as to destination and cause; nothing further about the term itself has been located. The 5 July date follows immediately from the arrest of the previous day and is not separately documented.
stops.campa: Upper Silesia, a prison at Ratibor on the Oder, three months for blasphemy against a religion that is not his own and that he has been accused of insulting by attacking its book. He had published on the mistreatment of soldiers and on the beating of children in schools. On this he publishes nothing. No account of the term survives, not from him and not from anyone else: no cell, no work detail, no visitor, no release date, no complaint. The Ratibor registers for 1900 have not been located.
suggested_refs: Prussian prison registers for Ratibor, 1900, not located
sources: Guttzeit's autobiographical notice in Der Neue Mensch, summer 1900

stops.name: Loschwitz, the journal fails and the house is broken up
stops.date_confidence: attested that Der Neue Mensch failed commercially and ended, and that Guttzeit moved to Upper Silesia in 1903 (de.wikipedia: '1903 verzog Guttzeit nach Oberschlesien'). The Upper Silesian destination is not further specified in any reachable source.
stops.campa: Der Neue Mensch does not pay and it stops. Three years, and the second of his two journals closes for want of subscribers rather than for want of argument; the Bruder-Bund had ended the same way, quietly, without a quarrel to explain it. In the same year he leaves the Elbe slope for Upper Silesia, the province that held his prison, and no source names the town he goes to. He is fifty. The pamphlets go on appearing, in other men's imprints now, and the robe is still on.
suggested_refs: Surviving runs of Der Neue Mensch, 1900-1903

stops.name: Upper Silesia, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. de.wikipedia gives '1903 verzog Guttzeit nach Oberschlesien und heiratete 1905 zum zweiten Mal', so the move and the marriage are two years apart and are separated here accordingly. No place of marriage is documented and no civil certificate has been located; the coordinate is a regional placeholder for Upper Silesia, not an attested site.
stops.campa: He marries for the second time somewhere in Upper Silesia. The bride is not named in any reachable source, the town is not named, and no certificate has been found, which is also true of the first marriage and of Alma. From here the wandering slackens. He is fifty-two, and nine years earlier he published a book arguing in the first person that marriage and free love are not opposites. The second household exists in one clause of one encyclopaedia article and in no register anyone has opened.
suggested_refs: Upper Silesian civil marriage registers, 1905, not consulted

stops.name: Leipzig, Ein dunkler Punkt at Max Spohr
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the first-edition date from contemporary legal bibliography, correcting the standard bibliographies, which date the work to 1922. The edition sequence given by that bibliography, a second soon after, a fourth by 1911, a fifth in 1914 and a sixth by 1919, is itself the argument against 1922.
stops.campa: Max Spohr of Leipzig, the publisher who printed the early homosexual emancipation literature, brings out Guttzeit's Ein dunkler Punkt, on the crime against germinating life, against abortion. The man who defended same-sex love, free love and the emancipation of women writes at length against this, and the two positions run off one root: his master term is Life, or Nature, not the autonomy of the person who has to decide. A second edition follows soon after, a fourth by 1911, a fifth in 1914, a sixth by 1919. The standard bibliographies date the first edition to 1922.
suggested_refs: Ein dunkler Punkt. Das 'Verbrechen gegen das keimende Leben' oder die Fruchtabtreibung (Max Spohr, Leipzig, 1905)
sources: contemporary legal bibliography of the abortion literature (alexandria.unisg.ch)

stops.name: Neu-Esting, the robe laid aside
stops.date_confidence: attested: 'Ab 1908 wohnte Guttzeit in Neu-Esting.' The coordinate is a corrected placeholder between Esting (48.2008 / 11.3086) and Olching town centre (48.2086 / 11.3356), Neu-Esting lying between them; the values circulating in the research pool sat up to three kilometres off.
stops.campa: At fifty-five he comes back to the country outside Munich, twenty-three years after walking out of Diefenbach's community forty kilometres to the south, and takes a house at Neu-Esting by Olching. He also takes off the robe. The haircloth, the sandals and the loose hair that Hauptmann had described in Zurich and a prosecutor had charged him over in 1890 are exchanged for the ordinary coat of a German author. It is the second time in his life he changes his clothes to change what he is. No source records a reason for it, or a date inside the year.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Guttzeit at gusto-graeser.info, including one dated 1914 in author's dress

stops.name: Neu-Esting, writing on Isadora Duncan
stops.date_confidence: attested that by 1908 Guttzeit was writing approvingly of Isadora Duncan, and that a dance historian places him as a German sex-radical in that context. The relation is one-directional: Duncan's own record contains no mention of Guttzeit, and no meeting or discipleship is documented. The June date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He writes approvingly of Isadora Duncan, whose bare feet and loose tunic have been scandalising the same German public that once charged him with gross nuisance for his own clothes. He reads her freedom of the body as an ethical achievement and not merely an aesthetic one, which is the reading he has been giving his own robe since 1885. The line runs one way. Duncan's record was checked for his name and does not contain it, and no meeting, letter or discipleship is documented anywhere.
suggested_refs: Edward Ross Dickinson, Dancing in the Blood (2017), chapter 'Art, Women, Liberation'
sources: Edward Ross Dickinson, Dancing in the Blood (2017)

stops.name: Neu-Esting, Schamgefühl, Anstand und Sittlichkeit
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A documented 1911 edition survives and scholarly bibliographic citation puts the work in circulation from 1908, correcting the familiar 1922 date. The 1908 first edition has not been checked against a copy.
stops.campa: Shame, Propriety and Morality, through several editions from about 1908, with a surviving printing from 1911. The 1908 first edition has not been seen; the familiar date of 1922 is too late by fourteen years. Twenty years of testing the proposition on his own body in public, and one prosecution for the results, come down to a question he puts from a village outside Munich, at fifty-eight, in an ordinary coat. Is an uncovered body indecent, or is the indecency a habit of the clothed, learned young and never once examined?
suggested_refs: Schamgefühl, Anstand und Sittlichkeit, 1911 edition
sources: scholarly bibliographic citation, working bibliography reconstruction

stops.name: Neu-Esting, Die Tyrannei der Mode
stops.date_confidence: the work and its 1914 date come from the working bibliography reconstructed from library catalogues.
stops.campa: The Tyranny of Fashion, twenty-four years after the state took him to court over what he had on. Its title and its date come from library catalogues and no copy has been checked, which is true of most of what he published. The polemic that began as a criminal charge finishes as a book: clothing is not decoration but instruction, worn daily, obeyed without being noticed, enforced by a power that will prosecute a man for stepping outside it. He is sixty, in a village on the Amper, wearing a coat like everybody else's.
suggested_refs: Die Tyrannei der Mode (1914)
sources: working bibliography reconstructed from library catalogues

stops.name: Neu-Esting, Schöpfung und Sündenfall
stops.date_confidence: attested: a copy of the Neu-Esting 1914 imprint survives at the Heinrich-Heine-Institut, Düsseldorf, catalogued within the estate library of the poet Karl Röttger, object HHI.NLB.4382. The June date orders the segment only; no month is given.
stops.campa: Thirty-two years after Unsinn und Unmoral im Alten Testament he publishes the same quarrel resolved differently. Schöpfung und Sündenfall: Buchstäblich und geistig, creation and the fall, literally and spiritually, a contribution to religious liberation. The Bible is not to be thrown out but read otherwise, along lines he takes from Swedenborg; conventional theology is attacked and the Theosophists are laughed at. The road runs church Christianity, natural religion, radical humanism, then this. It does not run to atheism. One copy of the Neu-Esting imprint survives at Düsseldorf, in the estate library of the poet Karl Röttger.
suggested_refs: Schöpfung und Sündenfall: Buchstäblich und geistig (Neu-Esting, 1914), Heinrich-Heine-Institut, object HHI.NLB.4382
sources: Heinrich Heine Institute holdings record, emuseum.duesseldorf.de

stops.name: Munich, the Kakaostube at Karlsplatz
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction resting on a single source: Erich Mühsam's diary entry for 15 July 1916. The diary is Mühsam's, not Guttzeit's, and the friend from Zurich is not named there.
stops.campa: The telephone rings in Erich Mühsam's flat and it is Guttzeit, asking him to come to the Kakaostube on Karlsplatz to meet a friend visiting from Zurich. Mühsam goes, partly because a visitor out of neutral Switzerland in the third summer of the war carries information that does not get through the German press. Guttzeit is sixty-three and supposedly retired to a village, and he is on the telephone to the most watched anarchist in Munich. The diary is Mühsam's. It does not give the friend's name, and it is the only source there is for the afternoon.
suggested_refs: Erich Mühsam, diary entry of 15 July 1916, muehsam-tagebuch.de

stops.name: Neu-Esting, the letter to Michael Georg Conrad
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: a surviving handwritten letter, catalogued in the Michael Georg Conrad papers at the Münchner Stadtbibliothek / Monacensia, Kalliope record DE-611-HS-1397315. Further correspondence by Guttzeit survives from 1920.
stops.campa: A letter in his own hand goes from Neu-Esting to Michael Georg Conrad, the naturalist novelist and founder of the Munich journal Die Gesellschaft, and survives in Conrad's papers. Its contents are not reproduced in the catalogue entry. What the entry proves is the address and the date: in the January of the worst winter of the war, the old nature-preacher is still writing to literary Munich from a village on the Amper. The same year he reissues Die Macht des Glaubens und des Willens.
suggested_refs: Michael Georg Conrad papers, Münchner Stadtbibliothek / Monacensia

stops.name: Olching, the letter to Wilhelm Walloth
stops.date_confidence: attested: the German national authority record (GND 116936053) registers a letter from Guttzeit to the writer Wilhelm Walloth postmarked 10 June 1927. An earlier working description of this as an unspecified autograph is corrected here.
stops.campa: He is seventy-three and writing to the novelist Wilhelm Walloth. The letter is postmarked the tenth of June and is the last dated act of his life that anyone has found. He has outlived the kingdom that commissioned him, the empire it became, the war that broke it and the revolution that followed, and he is eight years into a republic that will not last much longer either. After this the documentary trail stops. There are eight more years of him, and nothing at all in them.
suggested_refs: The Guttzeit letter to Wilhelm Walloth, 10 June 1927, GND 116936053
sources: Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek, authority record gnd/116936053

stops.name: Olching, the year without a day
stops.date_confidence: attested only to the year. The national authority file records the death as XX.XX.1935 at Olching, with day and month never established. Literaturport contradicts this outright, giving his death as 'after 1913, place unknown'; the contradiction between two respectable catalogue sources is flagged and not resolved. No grave, headstone, plaque or street name has been located anywhere.
stops.campa: He dies at Olching, aged eighty-one or eighty-two, in 1935. The national authority file, which fixed his birth to the day, records the death as XX.XX.1935 and has never been able to do better; one catalogue still has him dying after 1913 in an unknown place. Nothing marks the ground. No grave has been located at Olching, none at Esting, none at Loschwitz. What survives him is paper: a few hundred pamphlets on schoolrooms and soldiers and clothing and love, scattered through German libraries, and an apple breaking a sword on the covers.
suggested_refs: Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek authority record gnd/116936053, recording XX.XX.1935
